title: Reinforcement Learning: From Bandits to Policy Gradients
subtitle: Learn how agents learn from reward, from bandits and dynamic programming through Monte Carlo, TD learning, SARSA and Q-learning to deep Q-networks and policy gradients in PyTorch.
outcomes: Balance exploration and exploitation in bandit problems with ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling, and measure regret
Formulate problems as Markov decision processes and solve them with policy iteration and value iteration
Estimate values from experience with Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning
Learn control policies with SARSA and Q-learning, and explain how on-policy and off-policy methods differ
Explain how deep Q-networks stabilise learning, and train a policy-gradient agent with REINFORCE in PyTorch
prerequisites: Deep Learning with PyTorch (for the last module) and probability at the level of Statistics for Data Science and AI or Foundations of Probability and Statistics: expectations, conditional probability and sampling. Comfortable Python and NumPy. Install Python 3.10 or later with NumPy, PyTorch (pip install torch; the CPU build is enough) and Gymnasium (pip install gymnasium, for CartPole). Everything runs on a laptop CPU.
description:
Reinforcement learning is learning by trial and error: an agent acts, sees what happens and collects reward, and has to work out which of its actions led to the reward and which exploring is worth the cost. It's behind game-playing agents, robot controllers, recommendation and experimentation systems, and the fine-tuning of large language models from human feedback. This course builds it up in the standard order, each idea on the one before: bandits, Markov decision processes, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning, SARSA and Q-learning, and then deep Q-networks and policy gradients.

Every module has a lab that reproduces a classic experiment in code you complete yourself: exploration strategies on the 10-armed testbed, policy and value iteration on a slippery grid world, Monte Carlo against TD on the random walk, SARSA against Q-learning on the cliff, and REINFORCE on Gymnasium's CartPole in PyTorch. The capstone is a stock-control problem where dynamic programming gives the optimal policy, so you can measure exactly how close your learned agents get.

modules.title: Bandits: exploration and exploitation
modules.summary: Meet the reinforcement learning problem in its simplest form: choosing between options with uncertain rewards, and deciding when to try something new.

lessons.title: The reinforcement learning problem
objectives: Describe the agent-environment loop and the goal of maximising return
Explain how reinforcement learning differs from supervised learning
Define policies, value functions and models
key_points: In reinforcement learning an agent interacts with an environment: at each step it observes a state, takes an action, and receives a reward and the next state. Its goal is to maximise the total reward it collects over time, not the reward of any single step.

Unlike supervised learning, nobody provides the correct action: feedback says how good the chosen action was, not which was best; it can arrive many steps after the action that earned it; and the data the agent sees depends on the actions it takes.

A policy maps states to actions or to probabilities of actions; a value function predicts the future reward from a state, or from a state and an action; a model predicts the environment's next state and reward. Model-based methods plan with a model; model-free methods learn from experience alone.

Designing the reward is designing the task: an agent optimises exactly what the reward measures, so a reward that only approximates the goal invites behaviour that scores well and misses the point, often called reward hacking.

lessons.title: Multi-armed bandits and action values
objectives: Define a k-armed bandit and the value of an action
Estimate action values incrementally
Explain regret as a measure of performance
key_points: A k-armed bandit is reinforcement learning with a single state: each step the agent picks one of k actions and receives a random reward from that action's distribution. The action's value q*(a) is its expected reward; the best arm has the highest q*, but the agent only ever sees samples.

The sample-average estimate Q(a) is the mean of the rewards received from a, updated incrementally as Q ← Q + (R − Q)/n after the nth reward, so no history needs storing. Its form, new estimate = old + step size × (target − old), recurs throughout reinforcement learning.

A constant step size α weights recent rewards more than old ones (an exponential recency-weighted average), which suits nonstationary problems whose arms change over time; a step size of 1/n weights every reward equally and converges to the true mean for stationary arms.

Regret is the reward lost against always playing the best arm: the sum over steps of q*(best) − q*(chosen). The best strategies make total regret grow only logarithmically with time; exploring at a fixed rate makes it grow linearly.

steps.do: Update a sample average one reward at a time and compare it with the mean of all the rewards.

Q = 0.0
for n, r in enumerate(rewards, start=1):
    Q += (r - Q) / n
print(round(Q, 6), round(rewards.mean(), 6))

lessons.title: Exploration strategies
objectives: Compare greedy, ε-greedy and optimistic initial values
Explain how UCB and Thompson sampling direct exploration
Recognise where bandits are used in practice
key_points: Greedy selection always exploits the current estimates and can lock onto a poor arm after an unlucky start. ε-greedy explores at random with probability ε: simple and robust, but it keeps choosing bad arms at a fixed rate forever.

Optimistic initial values, such as Q0 = 5 when rewards are around 1, make every untried arm look attractive, so even a greedy agent tries them all early on. It helps on stationary problems and not on nonstationary ones, since all its exploration happens at the start.

Upper confidence bound (UCB) selection picks the arm that maximises Q(a) + c√(ln t / N(a)). The bonus is large for arms tried rarely and shrinks as N(a) grows, so exploration goes to the arms whose values are most uncertain.

Thompson sampling keeps a posterior over each arm's value, such as Beta(1 + successes, 1 + failures) for rewards of 0 or 1, draws one sample per arm and plays the highest. It explores in proportion to the probability that each arm is best, and often has the lowest regret in practice.

Bandits run online experiments, recommendations and ad selection. Contextual bandits choose using features of the current user or situation, for example with a linear model as LinUCB does, and sit between bandits and full reinforcement learning, where actions also change future states.

files.content:
"""Compare exploration strategies on a 10-armed testbed, then on Bernoulli bandits by regret.

Each of the 2,000 runs is its own bandit problem; all runs step together in NumPy arrays, so it takes seconds.
"""

import numpy as np

K, RUNS, STEPS = 10, 2000, 1000


def epsilon_greedy(Q, epsilon, rng):
    """One action per run: a random arm with probability epsilon, otherwise the arm with the highest estimate."""
    # TODO: draw a random arm for each run, then use it where rng.random(runs) < epsilon and the greedy arm
    #  (Q.argmax(axis=1)) elsewhere
    return Q.argmax(axis=1)


def ucb(Q, N, t, c):
    """Upper confidence bound: estimate plus c * sqrt(ln t / N); arms never tried come first."""
    # TODO: return the argmax over arms of Q + c * sqrt(ln(t) / N), treating N == 0 as an infinite bonus
    return Q.argmax(axis=1)


def testbed(strategy, seed=0, epsilon=0.0, q0=0.0, alpha=None, c=2.0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q_star = rng.normal(0, 1, (RUNS, K))
    best = q_star.argmax(axis=1)
    Q, N = np.full((RUNS, K), q0), np.zeros((RUNS, K))
    rewards, optimal = np.zeros(STEPS), np.zeros(STEPS)
    rows = np.arange(RUNS)
    for t in range(1, STEPS + 1):
        a = ucb(Q, N, t, c) if strategy == "ucb" else epsilon_greedy(Q, epsilon, rng)
        r = rng.normal(q_star[rows, a], 1)
        N[rows, a] += 1
        step = (1.0 / N[rows, a]) if alpha is None else alpha
        # TODO: the incremental update: move Q[rows, a] a fraction `step` of the way towards the reward r
        pass
        rewards[t - 1], optimal[t - 1] = r.mean(), (a == best).mean()
    return rewards, optimal


def bernoulli_regret(strategy, seed=0, runs=500, steps=5000):
    """Cumulative regret on 5-armed Bernoulli bandits: the reward lost against always playing the best arm."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    p = rng.uniform(0.1, 0.9, (runs, 5))
    rows = np.arange(runs)
    wins, plays = np.zeros((runs, 5)), np.zeros((runs, 5))
    regret = np.zeros(steps)
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        Q = np.divide(wins, plays, out=np.zeros_like(wins), where=plays > 0)
        if strategy == "thompson":
            a = rng.beta(wins + 1, plays - wins + 1).argmax(axis=1)   # sample from each Beta(1 + wins, 1 + losses)
        elif strategy == "ucb":
            a = ucb(Q, plays, t, np.sqrt(2))
        else:
            a = epsilon_greedy(Q, 0.1, rng)
        r = rng.random(runs) < p[rows, a]
        wins[rows, a] += r
        plays[rows, a] += 1
        regret[t - 1] = (p.max(axis=1) - p[rows, a]).mean()
    return regret.cumsum()


def main():
    print("== 1. 10-armed testbed: 2,000 runs, 1,000 steps")
    print(f"{'strategy':32} {'reward, steps 1-100':>20} {'reward, steps 901-1000':>23} {'optimal at the end':>19}")
    for name, kw in [("greedy", {"strategy": "eps"}),
                     ("epsilon-greedy, 0.01", {"strategy": "eps", "epsilon": 0.01}),
                     ("epsilon-greedy, 0.1", {"strategy": "eps", "epsilon": 0.1}),
                     ("optimistic greedy, Q0=5, a=0.1", {"strategy": "eps", "q0": 5.0, "alpha": 0.1}),
                     ("UCB, c=2", {"strategy": "ucb", "c": 2.0})]:
        rewards, optimal = testbed(**kw)
        print(f"{name:32} {rewards[:100].mean():20.3f} {rewards[-100:].mean():23.3f} {optimal[-100:].mean():19.1%}")
    print("== 2. Bernoulli bandits: cumulative regret (500 runs)")
    for name in ("epsilon-greedy", "ucb", "thompson"):
        regret = bernoulli_regret(name)
        print(f"{name:15} after 500 steps {regret[499]:6.1f}   after 5,000 steps {regret[-1]:6.1f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: Every array has one row per run: index with Q[rows, a] to update just the chosen arm in each run.
np.log(t) at t = 1 is 0, so arms already tried get no bonus on the first step; the infinite bonus makes sure each arm is tried once.
The regret numbers are averages over 500 runs; individual runs vary a lot.

modules.title: Markov decision processes and dynamic programming
modules.summary: Describe sequential decision problems as Markov decision processes, write their Bellman equations, and solve them exactly when the dynamics are known.

lessons.title: Markov decision processes
objectives: Define the parts of a finite MDP and the Markov property
Compute discounted returns
Write the Bellman expectation equation for a policy
key_points: A finite Markov decision process (MDP) has states, actions and dynamics p(s′, r | s, a): the probability of each next state and reward given the current state and action. The Markov property says that the current state holds everything about the past that matters for the future.

The return is the discounted sum of future rewards, G_t = R_{t+1} + γR_{t+2} + γ²R_{t+3} + …, with a discount factor γ from 0 to 1. γ < 1 keeps returns finite in continuing tasks and values sooner rewards more; episodic tasks end in a terminal state and can use γ = 1.

A policy π(a | s) gives the probability of each action in each state. Its state-value function v_π(s) is the expected return starting from s and following π; its action-value function q_π(s, a) is the expected return after taking a in s and following π afterwards.

The Bellman expectation equation writes each value in terms of the values one step later: v_π(s) = Σ_a π(a|s) Σ_{s′,r} p(s′, r | s, a)[r + γ v_π(s′)]. For a fixed policy that's a system of linear equations, one per state, which small MDPs can solve directly.

steps.do: Write down a three-state chain under a fixed policy: transition probabilities P and expected rewards r.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
P = np.array([[0.5, 0.5, 0.0],
              [0.0, 0.5, 0.5],
              [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]])     # state 2 is absorbing
r = np.array([-1.0, -1.0, 0.0])
gamma = 0.9

steps.do: Solve v = r + gamma P v as one linear system.
steps.code:
v = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(3) - gamma * P, r)
print(v.round(4))
steps.see: [-3.3058 -1.8182  0.    ]: each step costs 1 until the absorbing state.

steps.do: Get the same values by repeated sweeps, as iterative policy evaluation does.
steps.code:
V = np.zeros(3)
for sweep in range(1, 1000):
    new = r + gamma * P @ V
    if np.abs(new - V).max() < 1e-10:
        break
    V = new
print(sweep, V.round(4))
steps.see: 35 [-3.3058 -1.8182  0.    ]: the same values after 35 sweeps.

lessons.title: Optimal policies and the Bellman optimality equation
objectives: Define optimal value functions and optimal policies
Write the Bellman optimality equation
Explain why model-free control learns action values
key_points: The optimal value functions are v*(s) = max over policies of v_π(s), and q*(s, a) likewise. Every finite MDP has at least one deterministic optimal policy, and acting greedily with respect to q*, choosing argmax_a q*(s, a), is optimal.

The Bellman optimality equation, v*(s) = max_a Σ_{s′,r} p(s′, r | s, a)[r + γ v*(s′)], replaces the policy's average over actions with a maximum. The maximum makes it non-linear, so it's solved iteratively rather than as one linear system.
Small per-step rewards shape behaviour: a step cost pushes an agent to finish quickly, while the discount factor and the chance of slipping decide how wide a berth it gives dangerous states.

Knowing v* is enough to act optimally only with a model, because choosing an action needs a one-step lookahead through p(s′, r | s, a); knowing q* is enough without one, which is why model-free control methods learn action values.

lessons.title: Policy iteration and value iteration
objectives: Evaluate a policy iteratively
Improve a policy greedily, and iterate to the optimum
Compare policy iteration with value iteration
key_points: Iterative policy evaluation applies the Bellman expectation equation as an update to every state in turn (a sweep) until the largest change falls below a small threshold θ. With γ < 1, or when every policy eventually reaches a terminal state, it converges to v_π.

The policy improvement theorem says that acting greedily with respect to v_π gives a policy at least as good as π in every state. Policy iteration alternates full evaluation and greedy improvement until the policy stops changing, which takes finitely many iterations in a finite MDP.

Value iteration skips full evaluation: each sweep applies the Bellman optimality backup V(s) ← max_a Σ p(s′, r | s, a)[r + γV(s′)], and the greedy policy is read off at the end. Policy iteration takes a few expensive iterations, value iteration many cheap sweeps.

Dynamic programming needs a complete model, and one sweep costs time proportional to |S|² × |A|. Updating estimates from other estimates, called bootstrapping, carries over to the learning methods that follow, which do without the model.

modules.title: Learning from experience: Monte Carlo and TD
modules.summary: Estimate values without a model, from sampled episodes with Monte Carlo methods and from single steps with temporal-difference learning.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo prediction
objectives: Estimate state values by averaging sampled returns
Distinguish first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo
Explain Monte Carlo's bias, variance and limits
key_points: Monte Carlo methods estimate values from complete episodes of experience: a state's value is the average of the returns that followed visits to it. They need no model of the environment, only the ability to run episodes.
First-visit Monte Carlo averages the returns that follow the first visit to a state in each episode; every-visit Monte Carlo uses every visit. Both converge to v_π as the number of visits grows.

Monte Carlo targets are real returns, so the estimates are unbiased, but a return sums many random rewards and so has high variance. Updates must wait until the episode ends, which rules out continuing tasks and makes long episodes slow to learn from.
With a constant step size, V(S_t) ← V(S_t) + α[G_t − V(S_t)] tracks a changing policy or environment; a smaller α averages away more noise but learns more slowly.

walkthrough.title: Returns for first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo

steps.do: Compute the discounted return after every step of one episode, backwards.
steps.code:
states = ["A", "B", "A", "C"]
rewards = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 5.0]       # rewards received after leaving each state
gamma = 0.9
G, returns = 0.0, []
for r in reversed(rewards):
    G = r + gamma * G
    returns.append(round(G, 4))
returns.reverse()
print(list(zip(states, returns)))

steps.do: Collect the returns each method would average for state A.

first = every[:1]
print("first-visit:", first, "every-visit:", every)
steps.see: first-visit: [4.545] every-visit: [4.545, 4.5]: A was visited twice in this episode.

lessons.title: Temporal-difference learning
objectives: Apply the TD(0) update and compute the TD error
Compare TD and Monte Carlo targets
Describe n-step returns and TD(λ)
key_points: TD(0) updates after every step: V(S_t) ← V(S_t) + α[R_{t+1} + γV(S_{t+1}) − V(S_t)]. The bracket is the TD error δ_t. Its target uses the current estimate of the next state's value, so TD bootstraps, like dynamic programming, while learning from samples, like Monte Carlo.

A TD target depends on one random reward and one estimate, so it has much lower variance than a Monte Carlo return but is biased while the estimates are wrong. On many problems, such as the random walk in this module's lab, TD reaches a lower error for the same amount of experience.

TD learning works online, in continuing tasks and from incomplete episodes, because each update needs only one transition. For a fixed policy, tabular TD(0) converges to v_π with suitably decreasing step sizes.

n-step TD uses n real rewards and then bootstraps: G_{t:t+n} = R_{t+1} + … + γ^{n−1}R_{t+n} + γⁿV(S_{t+n}), between TD(0) at n = 1 and Monte Carlo at the episode's length. TD(λ) averages all the n-step returns with weights (1 − λ)λ^{n−1}, efficiently, using eligibility traces.

modules.title: Control: SARSA and Q-learning
modules.summary: Turn value estimates into better behaviour, learning action values on-policy with SARSA and off-policy with Q-learning, and see where each one shines.

lessons.title: From prediction to control
objectives: Describe generalised policy iteration
Explain why control without a model learns action values and must explore
Distinguish on-policy from off-policy learning
key_points: Generalised policy iteration describes almost every reinforcement learning control method: keep estimating the values of the current policy, and keep improving the policy towards acting greedily on those values, without waiting for either process to finish.

Without a model, control learns action values Q(s, a), because choosing the greedy action then needs only argmax_a Q(s, a). The policy must keep exploring, typically ε-greedily, or the values of untried actions are never learned.

On-policy methods learn the value of the policy they follow, exploration included. Off-policy methods learn the value of a different target policy, usually the greedy one, from data produced by an exploratory behaviour policy, which also lets them learn from old data or from other agents.

Schedules that are greedy in the limit with infinite exploration (GLIE), such as ε decaying towards 0 while every state-action pair keeps being visited, let tabular methods converge to the optimal action values and an optimal policy.

lessons.title: SARSA and Expected SARSA
objectives: Apply the SARSA update
Explain what an on-policy method's values include
Compare Expected SARSA with SARSA
key_points: SARSA updates Q(S, A) ← Q(S, A) + α[R + γQ(S′, A′) − Q(S, A)], using the action A′ the policy actually takes next; the quintuple (S, A, R, S′, A′) gives it its name. It's on-policy, so it learns the value of the ε-greedy policy it follows.

Because SARSA's values include the cost of its own exploration, it prefers actions that stay safe when an occasional random move happens: on the cliff-walking grid it learns a path away from the edge and earns more per episode while exploring than Q-learning does.

Expected SARSA replaces Q(S′, A′) with its expectation under the current policy, Σ_a π(a | S′) Q(S′, a), which removes the noise of sampling A′; it usually learns at least as well as SARSA and tolerates larger step sizes.

The step size trades speed against noise: with deterministic rewards and moves large steps work (this module's lab uses α = 0.5), while noisy environments need smaller ones. Optimistic initial action values encourage early exploration, as they do in bandits.

lessons.title: Q-learning
objectives: Apply the Q-learning update
Explain Q-learning's behaviour on the cliff
Recognise maximisation bias and how double learning removes it
key_points: Q-learning updates Q(S, A) ← Q(S, A) + α[R + γ max_a Q(S′, a) − Q(S, A)]. Its target uses the best action in the next state, whatever the agent does next, so it learns q* directly while behaving ε-greedily: it's off-policy.

Learning the greedy policy's values means Q-learning ignores the risk its own exploration creates: on the cliff it learns the shortest path, along the edge, which is optimal without exploration, but it falls off now and then while exploring, so its return during training is lower than SARSA's.

The maximum of noisy estimates is biased upwards (maximisation bias), so Q-learning overestimates uncertain values. Double Q-learning keeps two tables, choosing the next action with one and valuing it with the other, which removes the bias.

Tabular methods need a separate value for every state-action pair and learn nothing about states they haven't visited; large or continuous state spaces need function approximation, which brings instabilities of its own.

files.content:
"""SARSA against Q-learning on the cliff-walking grid: 4 x 12, start bottom left, goal bottom right, cliff between."""

import numpy as np

ROWS, COLS = 4, 12
START, GOAL = (3, 0), (3, 11)
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]          # up, right, down, left


def step(s, a):
    r, c = min(max(s[0] + MOVES[a][0], 0), ROWS - 1), min(max(s[1] + MOVES[a][1], 0), COLS - 1)
    if r == 3 and 0 < c < 11:                        # fell off the cliff: -100, back to the start
        return START, -100.0
    return (r, c), -1.0


def choose(Q, s, epsilon, rng):
    # TODO: epsilon-greedy: a random action with probability epsilon, otherwise the best action, breaking ties at
    #  random (rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(q == q.max())))
    return int(rng.integers(4))


def run(method, episodes=500, alpha=0.5, epsilon=0.1, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Q = np.zeros((ROWS, COLS, 4))
    returns = []
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, total = START, 0.0
        a = choose(Q, s, epsilon, rng)
        while s != GOAL:
            s2, r = step(s, a)
            total += r
            a2 = choose(Q, s2, epsilon, rng)
            # TODO: the target, with gamma = 1 and Q of the goal always 0. SARSA uses the action it will take next,
            #  Q[s2][a2]; Q-learning uses the best action, Q[s2].max(). Then update Q[s][a] towards the target
            pass
            s, a = s2, a2
        returns.append(total)
    return Q, np.array(returns)


def greedy_path(Q):
    s, path = START, [START]
    while s != GOAL and len(path) < 50:
        s, _ = step(s, int(Q[s].argmax()))
        path.append(s)
    grid = [["." for _ in range(COLS)] for _ in range(ROWS)]
    for c in range(1, 11):
        grid[3][c] = "C"
    for r, c in path:
        grid[r][c] = "o"
    return ["".join(row) for row in grid]


def main():
    print("Average return per episode over 50 runs (epsilon = 0.1, alpha = 0.5)")
    for method in ("sarsa", "q-learning"):
        results = [run(method, seed=seed) for seed in range(50)]
        returns = np.mean([r for _, r in results], axis=0)
        print(f"{method:11} episodes 1-50: {returns[:50].mean():7.1f}   episodes 401-500: {returns[400:].mean():6.1f}")
        print("   greedy path after training (run 0):")
        for line in greedy_path(results[0][0]):
            print("   " + line)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: SARSA must choose a2 before updating and then actually take it; the starter's loop already does this.
Ties are common at the start, when every Q is 0; breaking them always towards action 0 would bias the agent upwards.
Expected SARSA's target under ε-greedy: (1 - epsilon) * Q[s2].max() + epsilon * Q[s2].mean().

modules.title: Deep reinforcement learning
modules.summary: Scale up with neural networks: deep Q-networks and the tricks that keep them stable, policy gradients with REINFORCE, and actor-critic methods, using PyTorch and Gymnasium.

lessons.title: Function approximation and deep Q-networks
objectives: Explain semi-gradient Q-learning with a neural network
Describe the deadly triad
Explain experience replay, target networks and Double DQN
key_points: With function approximation, a model q(s, a; w) such as a neural network generalises across states. Semi-gradient Q-learning minimises (r + γ max_a′ q(s′, a′; w) − q(s, a; w))², treating the target as a constant, so gradients flow only through the prediction.

Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning together (the deadly triad) can make values diverge. Deep Q-networks (DQN, Mnih and colleagues, 2015) learned to play Atari games from screen pixels by adding two stabilisers to Q-learning: experience replay and a target network.

Experience replay stores transitions (s, a, r, s′, done) in a large buffer and trains on random minibatches from it, breaking up correlated consecutive steps and reusing each one many times. The target network is a copy of q that's updated only every so often, so the targets don't chase the predictions.

The details matter: a Huber loss limits the effect of large TD errors, ε decays from 1 to a small value, the target is r alone when s′ is terminal (not when a time limit merely truncated the episode), and Double DQN chooses the next action with the online network and values it with the target network.

walkthrough.title: The pieces of a DQN update

steps.do: Fill a replay buffer with random CartPole-shaped transitions and sample a minibatch.

import random
from collections import deque
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
random.seed(0)
buffer = deque(maxlen=10_000)
for _ in range(500):
    buffer.append((torch.randn(4), random.randrange(2), 1.0, torch.randn(4), random.random() < 0.05))
batch = random.sample(buffer, 32)
s, a, r, s2, done = zip(*batch)
s, s2 = torch.stack(s), torch.stack(s2)
a, r, done = torch.tensor(a), torch.tensor(r), torch.tensor(done, dtype=torch.float32)
print(len(buffer), tuple(s.shape), tuple(a.shape))

online = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))
target = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))

target.requires_grad_(False)

steps.do: Compute Double DQN targets without gradients (bootstrapping only where the episode didn't terminate) and the Huber loss.
steps.code:
gamma = 0.99
with torch.no_grad():
    next_a = online(s2).argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)          # choose with the online network
    next_q = target(s2).gather(1, next_a).squeeze(1)         # evaluate with the target network
    y = r + gamma * (1 - done) * next_q
q = online(s).gather(1, a.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)
loss = F.smooth_l1_loss(q, y)
loss.backward()
print(round(loss.item(), 4), online[0].weight.grad is not None, target[0].weight.grad is None)

lessons.title: Policy gradients and REINFORCE
objectives: Represent a stochastic policy with a network and torch.distributions
Derive the REINFORCE update from the policy gradient theorem
Reduce variance with a baseline
key_points: Policy-gradient methods learn a parametrised policy π(a | s; θ) directly, which suits stochastic policies and continuous actions. A network outputs logits, and torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=...) samples actions and returns their log-probabilities.

The policy gradient theorem makes the gradient of the expected return something an agent can sample: ∇J(θ) ∝ E[G_t ∇log π(A_t | S_t; θ)]. REINFORCE runs an episode, computes each step's return-to-go G_t and moves θ that way; in PyTorch, by minimising −Σ_t G_t log π(A_t | S_t).

REINFORCE's gradient is unbiased but very noisy. Subtracting a baseline b(S_t) that doesn't depend on the action, such as a learned state value or the mean return, leaves its expectation unchanged and can cut its variance a lot; normalising the returns within each episode is a common simple version.

Policy-gradient training is unstable: one large step can wreck a good policy, as the dips in this module's lab show. Smaller learning rates, more episodes per update, gradient clipping and an entropy bonus that stops the policy becoming deterministic too early all help.

lessons.title: Actor-critic methods and reinforcement learning in practice
objectives: Describe actor-critic methods and PPO
Use the Gymnasium environment interface correctly
Evaluate agents fairly
key_points: Actor-critic methods learn a policy (the actor) and a value function (the critic) together, using the critic's TD error or an advantage estimate, A(s, a) = q(s, a) − v(s), in place of the full return. They can update every step and have lower variance, at the cost of some bias; A2C runs several environments in parallel.

PPO (proximal policy optimisation) limits how far each update moves the policy by clipping the probability ratio π_new(a | s) / π_old(a | s) to the range [1 − ε, 1 + ε] in its objective. It's a common default for policy optimisation, including fine-tuning language models from human feedback.

Gymnasium is the standard Python interface to environments: env.reset(seed=...) returns (observation, info), and env.step(action) returns (observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info). terminated means the task ended, so bootstrap from 0; truncated means a time limit stopped it, so bootstrap as usual.

Evaluate agents honestly: results vary a lot between random seeds, so report the mean and spread over several seeds and many evaluation episodes, evaluate with exploration switched off, and compare with simple baselines and, where it can be computed, the optimum.

"""REINFORCE: learn to balance Gymnasium's CartPole with a policy network in PyTorch.

python reinforce.py                 # with returns normalised in each episode (a simple baseline)
python reinforce.py --no-baseline   # with raw returns
"""

import argparse

import gymnasium as gym
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.distributions import Categorical


def returns_to_go(rewards, gamma):
    """G_t = r_t + gamma * G_(t+1), for every step of one episode."""
    # TODO: walk the rewards backwards accumulating G = r + gamma * G, then return the values in forward order
    #  as a float32 tensor
    return torch.zeros(len(rewards))


def run_episode(env, policy, greedy=False):
    obs, _ = env.reset()
    log_probs, rewards, done = [], [], False
    while not done:
        dist = Categorical(logits=policy(torch.as_tensor(obs, dtype=torch.float32)))
        action = dist.probs.argmax() if greedy else dist.sample()
        obs, reward, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(int(action))
        log_probs.append(dist.log_prob(action))
        rewards.append(float(reward))
        done = terminated or truncated           # terminated: the pole fell; truncated: 500 steps reached
    return log_probs, rewards


def train(episodes, gamma, lr, baseline, seed):
    env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
    env.reset(seed=seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    policy = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))      # logits for left and right
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=lr)
    lengths = []
    for episode in range(1, episodes + 1):
        log_probs, rewards = run_episode(env, policy)
        G = returns_to_go(rewards, gamma)
        if baseline:
            G = (G - G.mean()) / (G.std() + 1e-8)
        # TODO: the REINFORCE loss is minus the sum over steps of log_prob * G; minimise it with the optimiser
        pass
        lengths.append(len(rewards))
        if episode % 100 == 0:
            print(f"episode {episode:4d}  mean return over the last 100 episodes {np.mean(lengths[-100:]):6.1f}")
    return policy


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--episodes", type=int, default=800)
    parser.add_argument("--no-baseline", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    policy = train(args.episodes, gamma=0.99, lr=0.01, baseline=not args.no_baseline, seed=0)
    env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
    env.reset(seed=1000)
    with torch.no_grad():
        scores = [sum(run_episode(env, policy, greedy=True)[1]) for _ in range(20)]
    print(f"greedy policy over 20 new episodes: mean return {np.mean(scores):.1f} (min {min(scores):.0f}, "
          f"max {max(scores):.0f}); CartPole-v1 counts as solved at 475")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: The loss is negative because optimisers minimise: minimising -log_prob * G raises the probability of actions followed by high returns.
torch.stack(log_probs) keeps the graph from every step; converting them to floats would cut it.
Results differ between seeds and machines; that's the point of the seed table.

files.content:
"""The capstone's environment: each evening, decide how many units to order for the next day.

State: units in stock at the start of the day, 0 to 20. Action: units to order, 0 to 10, delivered before the shop
opens (stock can't go above 20; anything beyond that is wasted). Each day's demand is Poisson with mean 3. The day's
profit is 5 per unit sold, minus 2 per unit ordered, minus 8 for placing any order at all, minus 0.3 per unit left in
stock overnight, minus 1 per unit of demand that couldn't be met. An episode is 100 days, starting with 5 in stock.

InventoryEnv follows Gymnasium's API (reset returns (state, info); step returns (state, reward, terminated,
truncated, info)), and transition_model() gives the exact probabilities for dynamic programming.
"""

import math

import numpy as np

MAX_STOCK, MAX_ORDER, MEAN_DEMAND, DAYS = 20, 10, 3.0, 100
PRICE, UNIT_COST, ORDER_COST, HOLDING, SHORTAGE = 5.0, 2.0, 8.0, 0.3, 1.0
N_STATES, N_ACTIONS = MAX_STOCK + 1, MAX_ORDER + 1


def day(stock, order, demand):
    """The next morning's stock and the day's profit."""
    available = min(stock + order, MAX_STOCK)
    sold = min(available, demand)
    left = available - sold
    profit = (PRICE * sold - UNIT_COST * order - (ORDER_COST if order > 0 else 0.0) - HOLDING * left
              - SHORTAGE * (demand - sold))
    return left, profit


class InventoryEnv:
    def __init__(self, days=DAYS, start_stock=5):
        self.days, self.start_stock = days, start_stock
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng()

    def reset(self, seed=None):
        if seed is not None:
            self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.stock, self.t = self.start_stock, 0
        return self.stock, {}

    def step(self, action):
        demand = int(self.rng.poisson(MEAN_DEMAND))
        self.stock, profit = day(self.stock, int(action), demand)
        self.t += 1
        return self.stock, profit, False, self.t >= self.days, {"demand": demand}


def transition_model(max_demand=30):
    """P[s][a]: a list of (probability, next_state, reward), one entry per possible demand."""
    probs = np.array([math.exp(-MEAN_DEMAND) * MEAN_DEMAND ** d / math.factorial(d) for d in range(max_demand + 1)])
    probs /= probs.sum()
    return [[[(float(p), *day(s, a, d)) for d, p in enumerate(probs)] for a in range(N_ACTIONS)]
            for s in range(N_STATES)]


def evaluate(policy, episodes=200, seed=1000):
    """Mean profit per day of a policy (a function from stock to order) over fixed simulated episodes."""
    env, totals = InventoryEnv(), []
    for e in range(episodes):
        s, _ = env.reset(seed=seed + e)
        total, done = 0.0, False
        while not done:
            s, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(policy(s))
            total += r
            done = terminated or truncated
        totals.append(total / env.days)
    return float(np.mean(totals)), float(np.std(totals) / np.sqrt(episodes))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for name, policy in [("never order", lambda s: 0),
                         ("order 3 every day", lambda s: 3),
                         ("below 4 in stock, order up to 8", lambda s: 8 - s if s < 4 else 0)]:
        mean, se = evaluate(policy)
        print(f"{name:32} mean profit per day {mean:6.2f} (standard error {se:.2f})")
